title: Where to Start with Venice
dek: Eight books, from first glance to the Rialto ledgers

slides.heading: Begin with the Mood
slides.body: James Morris, later Jan Morris, published *Venice* in 1960. Half travel book, half portrait, it makes no attempt to march through the dates. It is the book that makes you want the history.

art.title: The Grey Lagoon (Gondolas on the Lagoon)

slides.heading: Then the Whole Story
slides.body: John Julius Norwich first wrote *A History of Venice* in two volumes, 1977 and 1981, then merged them in 1982. Doges, plots and wars, from lagoon settlers to Napoleon ending the Republic in 1797.

slides.heading: A Merchant City Builds Empire
slides.body: Roger Crowley's *City of Fortune* (2011) follows the Stato da Mar, Venice's chain of ports and islands reaching to Crete and Cyprus. Includes 1204, when Venice helped sack Constantinople. Business, by other means.

slides.heading: The Best Modern Overview
slides.body: Thomas F. Madden's *Venice: A New History* (2012) is the single volume to keep on the shelf. His thread: a republic that survived for centuries by being relentlessly practical. It runs right up to the cruise ships.

art.title: The Bucintore Returning to the Molo on Ascension Day

slides.heading: The Historian's Foundation
slides.body: Frederic C. Lane spent a career on Venetian ships, merchants and state finance. *Venice: A Maritime Republic* (1973) is still the book specialists hand their students. Read it to see how trade actually worked.

art.title: The Miracle of the Relic of the Cross at the Ponte di Rialto

slides.heading: Down at the Shipyard
slides.body: The Arsenal was the state shipyard and one of preindustrial Europe's largest workplaces. Robert C. Davis's *Shipbuilders of the Venetian Arsenal* (1991) follows its workers, the arsenalotti: wages, privileges, pride. History from the slipway.

art.title: (Venice) Insegna dell'arte dei Calafati d'Arsenale - Correr Museum

slides.heading: How a Myth Was Staged
slides.body: Edward Muir's *Civic Ritual in Renaissance Venice* (1981) asks why Venice looked so stable to outsiders. His answer: ritual. Processions, feasts and the doge's Marriage of the Sea built the famous myth of Venice.

slides.heading: The Deep End
slides.body: Lane and Reinhold Mueller's *Money and Banking in Medieval and Renaissance Venice*, volume one (1985), unpicks coins and moneys of account. Come for the gold ducat, first minted in 1284. Stay for the bookkeeping.

caption:
Every Ascension Day, the doge of Venice sailed out, dropped a ring into the sea and declared it his bride.

That ceremony tells you a lot about Venice: a city that ran on trade and loved to put on a show. Its archives are huge, and Venetian ambassadors' reports, the relazioni, are still read by historians of courts across Europe. This list goes from easy reading to the hard stuff.

Further reading: Frederic C. Lane, *Venice: A Maritime Republic*; Roger Crowley, *City of Fortune*; Edward Muir, *Civic Ritual in Renaissance Venice*

risk_notes: Norwich publication history: originally *Venice: The Rise to Empire* (1977) and *Venice: The Greatness and the Fall* (1981), merged as *A History of Venice* in 1982. Defend by citing both original titles.
Ducat first minted 1284 is standard (under Doge Giovanni Dandolo). If challenged, note it is the conventional date in Lane and Mueller.
Arsenal as 'one of the largest workplaces' in preindustrial Europe: phrased as 'one of', which is widely accepted; avoid giving a worker headcount.
Stato da Mar 'reaching to Crete and Cyprus': Crete was held from the early 1200s, Cyprus only from 1489. If challenged, clarify the holdings changed over time.
Republic's span: tradition dates the first doge to 697, but the early doges are partly legendary, so the slide avoids an exact age.
Morris published as James Morris in 1960 and later wrote as Jan Morris. Handle respectfully: say 'published under the name James Morris'.

issues.problem: "first wrote *A History of Venice* in two volumes, 1977 and 1981" suggests the two volumes carried that title. They were published as *Venice: The Rise to Empire* (1977) and *Venice: The Greatness and the Fall* (1981). The combined *A History of Venice* came out in 1982. A pedant in the comments will catch this.
issues.fix: "John Julius Norwich wrote Venice's story in two volumes (1977 and 1981), then merged them as *A History of Venice* in 1982." Recount the body afterwards to keep it within 22 to 40 words.

issues.problem: The heading "The Best Modern Overview" and the line "is the single volume to keep on the shelf" state a matter of taste as settled fact. Norwich and Lane are strong rivals for that spot.
issues.fix: Heading: "A Sharp Modern Overview". Body: "is a strong single volume to keep on the shelf."

issues.problem: "His answer: ritual... built the famous myth of Venice" overstates Muir's argument. In his account, civic ritual expressed and reinforced a myth that also had literary and political roots, some of them older than many of the ceremonies. Ritual didn't create the myth on its own.
issues.fix: "His answer: ritual. Processions, feasts and the doge's Marriage of the Sea helped sustain the famous myth of Venice."

issues.problem: "is still the book specialists hand their students" is a fair point but stated as a universal. It's minor, and softening it costs nothing.
issues.fix: "is still a book specialists hand their students."
